antarctica-claimed.essay:
Antarctica covers 14,200,000 square kilometres, and seven countries say parts of it belong to them. Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the United Kingdom hold eight separate claims, drawn mostly as wedges running to the South Pole. France dates its claim to 1840, and Britain's dates to 1908, when it said it needed to regulate and tax whaling. The claims of Argentina, Chile and Britain overlap. Most other countries do not recognise any of them, and the United States and Russia keep the right to make claims of their own. For a person wondering about setting up on the ice, the first thing to understand is that this argument was deliberately frozen.

The freeze comes from the Antarctic Treaty, signed by twelve countries in Washington on 1 December 1959 and in force since 23 June 1961. It governs everything south of 60 degrees South, including ice shelves, and rights on the high seas in the area remain. It now has 58 members, of which 29 are Consultative, meaning they take part in decisions, and 29 are Non-Consultative. Article I allows peaceful purposes only, with no military bases or exercises. Article IV is the heart of it. Under IV(1), no member gives up or loses its claim or its position on anyone else's claim. Under IV(2), acts or activities while the treaty is in force cannot support or deny a claim or "create any rights of sovereignty", and no new claim may be asserted. Sovereignty means the legal right to rule a place. The effect resembles two neighbours who agree to stop arguing over a boundary and agree that nothing either does in the meantime will count in the argument.

This means that the usual way of winning land by living on it does not work here. Chile and Argentina have tried harder than anyone. In February 1984 Chile moved families to Villa Las Estrellas on King George Island, beside an air base, with a school, civil registry, post office and bank. Juan Pablo Camacho, born there that November, received life insurance and study funding from Augusto Pinochet at a ceremony in the presidential palace, and the local radio station is named Radio Soberanía, meaning sovereignty. Argentina flew Silvia Morella de Palma to Esperanza Base when she was seven months pregnant, and her son Emilio Palma was born there on 7 January 1978. Some sources count 11 births on the continent. Article IV says none of this can build a legal claim. Two governments placing families, schools and registers on the ice have gained nothing in treaty law from doing it, and a private group would have much less standing than either of them.

Practical access runs through governments as well. Article VII(5) requires each member to give advance notice of all expeditions organised by its nationals or from its territory, and of its ships. Members of the Madrid Protocol, a treaty added to the Antarctic Treaty to protect the environment, must also assess the environmental impact of such activities beforehand under Article 8. Article 7 bans any activity relating to mineral resources other than science. So the country of your passport or your departure port is the practical limit. In practice, treaty countries issue the permits. Australians need an environmental assessment approved by the Australian Antarctic Division, and New Zealand requires government approval to visit the Ross Dependency. Britain requires a permit for anyone on an expedition organised in the UK or leaving from it, and for British-flagged ships, and it asks for applications at least four months ahead for a new or unusual trip. Organisers must be self-sufficient and able to handle emergencies such as oil spills. About 124,000 cruise visitors came in 2025, and around 30 yachts visit the Peninsula each year, all of which is visiting and gives no one a claim. These rules are enforced. Jarle Andhøy, a Norwegian skipper, sailed to Antarctica in 2012 on the yacht Nilaya without authorisation, after the Norwegian Polar Institute had held up an earlier trip because he had not supplied information on his activities and insurance. A Norwegian district court convicted him in June 2014 and fined him 45,000 kroner, about $7,000, rejecting his argument that the rules did not apply because he never landed. The Treaty does not address private ownership of land, and nothing in it gives a private person a way to hold ground. Claimant countries may treat a sector as theirs, while other members are free not to recognise that under Article IV(1)(c). A settler could therefore face the law of a home country, a departure country and a claimant all at once.

Then there are the physical facts. At Villa Las Estrellas about 150 people live in summer and 80 in winter, with a nearest major hospital over 1,000 kilometres away, and BBC Future reported in 2018 that residents on long stays have their appendix removed before coming. All of this rests on a Chilean military air base. A private settlement would have to bring in its own fuel, food and transport, and no one is obliged to supply them. Any rescue would come from a government station or a ship, on that government's terms.

The closest thing to a private base is Greenpeace's World Park Base at Cape Evans on Ross Island, in the sector New Zealand claims. It ran year-round from 1987 to 1992 and remains the only non-government year-round base. Greenpeace wanted a voice at treaty meetings and wanted to stop mining. Treaty governments officially ignored it and gave it no help, though New Zealand would have helped in an emergency. The countries were negotiating a treaty to allow regulated mining at the time. Australia and France withdrew from it, it failed to gain enough support by its deadline of 25 November 1989, and the Madrid Protocol was agreed in 1991 and came into force in 1998. Having met its aim, Greenpeace removed the base in 1991 and 1992. A study in Polar Record estimated total fuel spills at under 200 litres, with contamination in one spot reaching 70 centimetres into frozen ground. So a well funded organisation with ships and public support held a camp for five years, as a campaign. It claimed no land and it took the base away.

Some misunderstandings are common. Many people believe the mining ban expires on a set date. The Madrid Protocol's Article 25(2) lets any Consultative Party call a review conference once 50 years have passed since the protocol took effect, which by simple arithmetic falls in January 2048, and that is a right to call a conference, which is not an expiry date. Another is that a country outside the treaty, or a citizen of one, is free to act as they like. The treaty binds its members. But an individual from outside it is still a national of some country, most routes pass through a member's territory, and Article IV(2)'s wording on "any rights of sovereignty" would be applied by member countries to any new claim. A third is that Marie Byrd Land, the unclaimed sector, escapes all this. It does not, since new claims are barred there too.

A person who wanted to do something real here could join a national research programme or a permitted expedition, or work with a group trying to shape treaty meetings, as Greenpeace did. Someone leaving from a treaty member's territory would be notified to other members by that country, with an impact assessment if it has joined the Madrid Protocol. Those paths give access and sometimes influence. They do not give any right over the land. The odds reflect this, with the chance of building at about 5 percent and of holding at about the same, and recognition close to nothing. Access is hard to arrange independently, and the treaty has closed the legal route for as long as it stays in force.

antarctica-unclaimed.essay:
Almost all of Antarctica is claimed by one country or another, but one large wedge has no claimant. It runs from 90 degrees West to 150 degrees West and is mostly called Marie Byrd Land, about 1,610,000 square kilometres including the Eights Coast. It is the largest unclaimed land on Earth. Norway's tiny Peter I Island, at about 90 degrees 35 minutes West, lies inside that band and is the one exception. This wedge attracts people looking for empty ground, and a number of them have announced countries there from their homes. To see why those announcements have no legal effect, it helps to start with how land used to be claimed and what changed.

Countries used to gain land by finding and occupying a place that belonged to no one. Lawyers call such a place terra nullius, Latin for nobody's land. Seven countries staked out parts of Antarctica, most of them between 1908 and the 1940s. Nobody claimed this sector, which Wikipedia calls remote even by Antarctic standards. The Antarctic Treaty was signed in 1959 and took effect in 1961, and it governs everything south of 60 degrees South. Article IV(2) says that "no new claim, or enlargement of an existing claim" may be asserted while the treaty is in force. It also says acts during the treaty cannot create rights of authority over the land. So the old method was shut off just as this wedge was left over.

Someone usually objects at this point that the treaty binds only countries that joined it, and that it does not stop an individual. That is right as far as it goes. The treaty binds its 58 members, and the idea that acts by someone outside it cannot create rights is an interpretation. Applying it to individuals does not depend on the treaty alone, though. A private person is still a national of some country, and only countries have ever made claims of this kind in the way international law recognised. A person with no state behind them has no standing to claim territory, since the old occupation method was one used by countries. In its Western Sahara opinion, the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, treated it as a method used by states. If a citizen of a treaty member went to this sector, that country's own permit rules would apply. Under Britain's rules, for example, anyone on an expedition organised in the UK or leaving from it needs a permit. Norway's rules caught the skipper Jarle Andhøy, whom a Norwegian court fined 45,000 kroner in 2014 for sailing to Antarctica without authorisation in 2012, even though he said he never landed. An individual from a country outside the treaty would still most likely travel through a treaty member's territory.

Getting there is where the legal rules become practical. Article VII(5) requires members to give notice of expeditions organised by their nationals or from their territory. The Madrid Protocol, an add-on to the treaty that protects the environment, applies here as in the claimed sectors. Article 3 sets environmental principles, Article 7 bans mining, and Article 8 requires an impact assessment beforehand. Most routes pass through the territory of a treaty member, whose government would have to notify the others. So the same limits apply as in the claimed sectors, and the absence of a claimant does not create an open door. The United States and Russia say they keep the right to make claims later, according to Wikipedia, which marks one of those two statements as needing a citation, and either might object to a settler in a sector they could one day claim.

The physical challenge is at least as large. A settlement would need fuel, food and shelter for a continent where even Chile's Villa Las Estrellas, a government settlement on an island near the mainland beside an air base, has a major hospital over 1,000 kilometres away and asks long-stay residents to have their appendix removed before they come. Marie Byrd Land is far more remote. Food, water and power would all have to be flown or shipped in, and the mining ban rules out paying for it from the ground. If something went wrong, the people who came would be the nearest government station's rescue problem, and that government would then be involved. Medical care, schooling and inheritance would all stay under the law of a person's own country.

The real cases show how these claims work in practice. The Grand Duchy of Westarctica was declared in 2001 by Travis McHenry, a US Navy intelligence specialist who read in the CIA World Factbook that no state had claimed the land. He wrote to many countries, and only other micronations, meaning tiny self-declared countries, responded. By 2006 his Navy superiors knew he was writing to foreign governments and told him to choose, and he kept his job and handed the title to a friend. He began issuing fantasy passports as souvenirs in 2004 and stopped after learning that a scammer in Kenya was selling them to refugees as real travel documents. In July 2025 Indian police arrested Harsh Vardhan Jain for running a fake Westarctica embassy from a rented house in Ghaziabad. In 2014 Westarctica registered as a non-profit, and it now campaigns on climate. It has no one on the land.

The Grand Duchy of Flandrensis, started by Niels Vermeersch of Belgium in 2008 as a two-week hobby, claims five islands off this coast, Siple, Cherry, Maher, Pranke and Carney. It registered in Belgium as a non-profit in 2021 and counted 741 citizens of 71 nationalities. It says it does not seek diplomatic recognition and does not intend to visit. Its founder spoke at a climate summit in Paris in 2022. The Kingdom of Talossa, begun by a 14-year-old in Milwaukee in 1979, includes part of Marie Byrd Land in its claim along with the east side of Milwaukee. It counted 157 active citizens in 2023, and none live on the Antarctic land. None of the three has built anything or been tested in any court, and the claims have stayed untested because nobody has gone there.

These cases show what can actually be accomplished. Such a project can be a website, a non-profit, a climate campaign or a hobby community registered under the law of the founder's own country. Those are real activities with real members, and they can draw attention to melting ice. They bring no land rights. The risks that have actually appeared are the ones found in any self-declared country. Passports get misused by others, officials or employers take an interest, and someone may use the name for fraud.

The most workable version keeps these limits in view. A person could register a non-profit at home, publish a clear statement that its papers are not travel documents, and take part in climate or polar education. A person who wanted to stand on the land would have to join an expedition that follows notice and impact rules from a treaty member. The odds reflect the position, with about a 5 percent chance of building anything, about 10 percent for holding it, and a fraction of one percent for recognition. Marie Byrd Land being unclaimed has not made it available, since the same treaty that froze the existing claims closed this sector to new ones.

buffer-zones.essay:
When two armies stop fighting, they often agree to pull back from each other and leave a strip of land between them, so that a stray shot or a patrol does not restart the war. That strip is a buffer zone. Because no army is meant to hold it, it can look on a map like land that belongs to nobody, and people interested in empty places sometimes wonder whether a new territory could be set up there. It cannot, and the reasons say a good deal about how ceasefires work. The surrounding countries, or the parties to the ceasefire, keep their claims. A peacekeeping force or a ceasefire body controls entry. The strip is an arrangement between the two sides, and the land inside still belongs to someone in law.

The Korean Demilitarized Zone is the most guarded example. It was created by the armistice, or ceasefire agreement, of 27 July 1953. Under it, each side moved back 2,000 metres from the front line, leaving a zone about 4 kilometres wide and about 250 kilometres long. Only two villages are allowed to remain inside. Daeseong-dong, also called Tae Sung Dong or Freedom Village, is on the southern side, governed and protected by the United Nations Command. It had 218 people in 2008, descended from those who owned the land before the war. They must generally spend at least 240 nights a year there to keep their residency. They count as South Korean citizens and do not pay tax or do military service. Kijŏng-dong, or Peace Village, is on the northern side. Only North Korea or the UN Command can give access. In January 2026 the UN Command strongly opposed South Korean bills that would give Seoul authority over non-military entry, calling them completely at odds with the armistice and stressing its role as the zone's administrator. If South Korea's own lawmakers meet that response, a private founder has little room. Those villagers' special position comes from the armistice and from their families' earlier ownership of the land. A newcomer has no route in, and the edges of the zone are among the most heavily armed borders in the world.

The UN Buffer Zone in Cyprus, also called the Green Line, shows a much more lived-in version. It began in 1964 and was extended after the ceasefire of 16 August 1974, which followed the Turkish invasion and split the island. It runs 180 kilometres across the island and covers 346 square kilometres, ranging from under 20 metres wide in places to over 7 kilometres, and it cuts through the capital, Nicosia. The UN force in Cyprus patrols it. About 10,000 people live and farm in villages inside it, including Deneia, Athienou and Troulloi. Pyla is the only village, by the UN force's account, where Greek and Turkish Cypriots live side by side. The UN divides the zone into two kinds of ground. In the Civil Use Areas, which include these villages, people may enter freely. Everywhere else, civilian activity needs specific authorisation from the UN force, which weighs security, ownership and its own operations when dealing with civilian building. It handles about 1,000 incidents a year. These are people who were already there, or their descendants, and they remain citizens of an existing country. Crossing was very limited until April 2003, when the Turkish Cypriot administration eased its restrictions after nearly 30 years.

A person might assume that such a mixed village, in a place neither side fully governs, would be a good place to declare something new. No one has been reported trying to declare a separate state in the zone, and small events show how closely the ground is watched. In 2009 UN troops stopped villagers in Mammari, a Civil Use Area, from gathering wild asparagus in nearby fields, saying the fields were in a restricted area near Turkish military outposts. Access to restricted ground required a request to the UN. In August 2023 de facto Turkish security forces attacked UN peacekeepers near Pyla in a dispute over unauthorised construction, seriously injuring three, and the Security Council called it a violation of the status quo, meaning the existing situation that is meant to stay unchanged. In 1996 two Greek Cypriot protesters were killed during protests against the division, one beaten and one shot while climbing a flagpole. A newcomer's building or flag would land in that setting, and it would need authorisation from a force whose job is to prevent changes.

The Chernobyl Exclusion Zone is a different kind of no-go strip. It was emptied because of radiation, with no army line involved. The 30-kilometre zone in Ukraine and Belarus was evacuated after the 1986 nuclear disaster, about 100,000 people in all. About 1,200 people returned in 1986. They are called samosely, meaning self-settlers. Most were elderly people who had lived there before the disaster. Many had been told they could go home in a few days, and they then faced discrimination in the areas where they were resettled. Some outsiders came too. Ukraine's government has not legalised their settlements, because living in the zone remains prohibited. A bill backed by Ukraine's parliament at first reading proposed fines of 17,000 to 42,500 hryvnia or restriction of freedom for illegal entry, and whether it passed in that form is not known. A minister said in 2013 that they receive full social support, and local officials have unofficially let elderly settlers stay.

The samosely show what tolerance looks like. Officials look away because the people are old, few and doing no harm, and because the state already pays them social support. They depend on the same state for help, which leaves them far from independent. Their number has fallen mainly through old age, from 314 in a 2007 census to 135 in 2017, and a Ukrainian report in April 2026 put the number left at about 25. Russian forces occupied the area in 2022, and residents have described that time as frightening. None of them has declared a separate state, and they remain residents of the countries that run the zone.

Several misunderstandings are worth clearing up. One is that a ceasefire strip is a gap in sovereignty, the legal right to rule a place. A ceasefire only pauses a fight, and the claims remain in place on both sides. Another is that peacekeepers are a kind of government that could be persuaded to let a project go ahead. Their job is to keep the two sides apart under the terms given to them, and they have no power to give away land. A third is that a place with no tax, like the Korean village, is free of the state. Its residents hold those exemptions because of special rules from an armistice, and they are still South Korean citizens. A fourth is that physical emptiness means legal emptiness. Chernobyl has been sealed for 40 years, and two governments still run it.

The risks of trying are serious. In the Korean zone, entry without permission means walking into a military frontier. In Cyprus, unauthorised activity outside the Civil Use Areas meets UN patrols, and the 2023 clash at Pyla shows how quickly construction can involve armed forces. At Chernobyl, living in the zone is prohibited, and the radiation that emptied it remains a health issue for anyone new.

There is no way to set up a self-governing territory here. The realistic options are to study or visit where that is allowed, and to work with those trying to reduce tension, such as the bicommunal life of Pyla. People do live in these zones, under peacekeepers or military authorities, and that leaves no room for a new government. For that reason the chances of building something are put at about 10 percent, law and holding at the same low level, and recognition at a tenth of a percent. Nothing in the known record gives a legal basis for self-rule in such a place.

buy-from-a-state.essay:
Buying a house and buying a country sound like larger and smaller versions of the same act. In law they are two different things. When someone buys land, they get ownership, which is the right to use it, fence it and sell it. The right to make the laws on that land, run its courts and collect its taxes is a separate thing called sovereignty, and it stays with the government. A person who owns a whole island still pays that country's taxes. The two can move separately. A classic American Journal of International Law article by Sayre explains that when a territory changes rulers, private owners generally keep their land while political authority passes to the new ruler. Sovereignty moves only when one government agrees to hand it to another, normally by treaty. So the selling country keeps authority until a treaty moves it to the buyer.

Countries have done this many times. The United States paid France $15 million for Louisiana in 1803, about 2,140,000 square kilometres. It paid Russia $7.2 million for Alaska in 1867, about 1,717,856 square kilometres. It paid Denmark $25 million in 1916 for the 400 square kilometres of the Danish West Indies. The most recent sale on Wikipedia's list of such purchases is Gwadar, which Pakistan bought from Muscat and Oman for £3 million in 1958. Every buyer and seller on that list is a country or a country-like ruler, and the list leaves out leases. A private buyer has no treaty partner, because a treaty is an agreement between states.

The first obstacle is that a government has to be willing to sell, and governments almost always refuse. The United States has tried to buy Greenland several times, including a secret offer of $100 million in gold in 1946, which Denmark rejected. When President Trump raised it in 2019, the Danish prime minister called the idea absurd. Under section 21 of Greenland's Self-Government Act, independence is for the Greenlandic people to decide, followed by negotiation with Denmark and a referendum, so the decision does not rest with one government alone. A September 2026 security agreement involved no sale. Sultan Abdul Hamid II told Theodor Herzl in 1896 that he could not sell a foot of land.

Private attempts have gone the same way. The founders of Minerva and Operation Atlantis looked for a government willing to sell and found none. Anton Bakov, a Russian businessman whose Romanov Empire project issued passports online, talked with several countries, and as of 2017 his talks with Kiribati and the Gambia had failed. Freedonia tried to lease land in Somaliland in 2001 and was rejected. No private purchase in the 20th or 21st century is known to have produced sovereignty.

Readers often point out that private buyers did get ruling rights in the past, and this is true. The Liechtenstein family paid 115,000 guilders for Schellenberg and 290,000 for Vaduz because it needed land directly under the emperor to earn a seat in the Imperial Diet. The emperor joined them into a principality in 1719, and it became sovereign in 1806 when Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine took it out of the empire. The Sultan of Brunei granted James Brooke land in Sarawak in 1841, and his family ruled as Rajahs until 1946. The British North Borneo Company bought concessions from the Sultans of Brunei and Sulu in 1877 and 1878, issued laws and set up courts, and handed the territory to Britain in 1946. King Leopold II of Belgium held the Congo Free State as a personal possession from 1885 to 1908, a regime of forced labour and mass death that ended when an international campaign led Belgium to annex it. Each of these rested on an emperor, sultan, king or great power willing to agree, and on an age when empires gave such grants. The North Borneo Company still needed a British royal charter, and it sold out to Britain for £860,000 in 1946. The Hudson's Bay Company held Rupert's Land, about a third of present-day Canada, under a 1670 charter, granted Lord Selkirk 300,000 square kilometres of it in 1811, and sold it through the Crown for £300,000 in 1869, while sovereignty lay with the Crown throughout. The Knights of Malta bought four Caribbean islands in 1651 with the French king keeping the final right to rule, and sold them in 1665. Jacques du Parquet bought Martinique in 1650, and the king revoked such sales in 1664. The Duchess of Atholl sold the lordship of Man to the Crown for £70,000 in 1765, which took an Act of Parliament. Sark's fief was sold in 1852 with the Queen's permission.

That earlier era also shows who was left out. Many of these purchases were made from peoples who did not understand the terms or who were later told they had no right to sell. Adolf Lüderitz bought coastal land in what is now Namibia in 1883, describing its width in German miles of about 7.4 kilometres to a chief who understood the English mile of 1.6, and Germans called it the Mile Swindle. Lobengula signed the Rudd Concession in 1888 and spent the next years trying to disown it. In Johnson v. M'Intosh in 1823, the US Supreme Court ruled that private buyers could not get good title from the Piankeshaw, because only the government holding sovereignty could buy out Native occupants. In 1835 the Governor of New South Wales declared John Batman's deal with Aboriginal elders for 600,000 acres near today's Melbourne void against the Crown. Virginia and North Carolina cancelled Richard Henderson's purchase from the Cherokee and paid him in land grants.

Today the normal result of buying land is ordinary ownership, and sometimes a very long lease. The Clunies-Ross family owned the Cocos Islands under an 1886 Crown grant while Britain and then Australia ruled them, and Australia paid A$6.25 million for most of their property in 1978. Firestone took up to a million acres of Liberia for 99 years in 1926, and the Golden Triangle zone in Laos runs on a 99-year lease in Lao territory. Kiribati, an actual country, paid $8.6 million in 2014 for about 22 square kilometres of Fiji, and it holds the land as an ordinary owner under Fijian law. Larry Ellison bought 98 percent of Lānaʻi in 2012 for $300 million, and it remains part of Hawaii. The Robinson family keeps Niʻihau closed to most outsiders, and it is still counted within Kauaʻi County. Palmyra Atoll shows how strong private title can be and where it stops. The US government sued the Fullard-Leo family, claiming the atoll had never been private, and the family won at the Supreme Court in 1947, yet the atoll was under US sovereignty the whole time. Martin Coles Harman, owner of Lundy, issued his own coins in 1929 and was convicted, and the High Court upheld that in 1931 because Lundy was part of England.

Even plain ownership can meet resistance if the purchase is large or held by foreigners. Iceland's law bars big purchases by outsiders, and its minister refused Huang Nubo an exemption in 2011 for about 300 square kilometres. Douglas Tompkins's Pumalín Park in Chile ran from the Pacific to the Argentine border, and parliament debated whether he was undermining sovereignty. Madagascar's new leader cancelled Daewoo's 99-year farm deal in 2009 after the protests that helped bring down his predecessor. The Solomon Islands Attorney-General declared a provincial lease of Tulagi unlawful in 2019. Satoshi Island's token sale in Vanuatu collapsed in 2025 because of a breach of the land lease, and Vanuatu had already said that a token gave no right of residence.

Selling is itself a legal hazard for a founder. Gregor MacGregor sold land and bonds in a country called Poyais that did not exist, and about two-thirds of the settlers who sailed there in 1822 and 1823 died. Selling shares in a future country can count as selling securities, as Lazarus Long's New Utopia found when the US Securities and Exchange Commission sued him in 1999 over a $350 million bond offering that had raised $24,000.

The workable version is modest. A person can buy an island or a ranch, pay the taxes, run it privately under the rules of the host country and write whatever charter they please for their own members. If a government did give up land by treaty to a new government, the title would be strong and hard to undo, and a treaty handover would answer the usual objection to a new state. That is why legal standing and the ability to hold such land rate highly in this route while the chance of it happening at all stays near one percent. No such deal is known, and a government would need a reason to give one that outweighs the anger seen in Egypt in 2016, when the transfer of Tiran and Sanafir to Saudi Arabia set off the largest protests against the government since 2014.

add_sources.t: Sayre, Change of Sovereignty and Private Ownership of Land, American Journal of International Law

host-state-carve-outs.essay:
A country can, if it chooses, set aside part of its own land and give it different rules. It might have separate business courts, lower taxes, its own regulators or even a form of self-government. This is the one route to separate rules that starts with the consent of the government in charge, and that is why it has actually worked. The host country keeps full authority unless it gives the land away by treaty, and the grant usually comes through its ordinary laws. What one legislature grants, a later court or legislature may take back. A person who follows this route is making an arrangement with a government and accepting that government's final word.

The best working example is the Dubai International Financial Centre, a business district of 110 hectares in the United Arab Emirates. In 2004 a federal law allowed each emirate to set up legal structures for financial centres, and Dubai then passed one law creating the centre and another creating its courts, which began working in 2006. Inside the zone, civil and commercial cases follow common law, the English system built on past court rulings, and they are heard in English, apart from the rest of the country's legal system. The centre has its own financial regulator and offers companies a 50-year guarantee of zero tax on corporate income. Other laws, such as criminal law and immigration rules, still apply. It is a place to do business under different commercial rules, and it remains part of Dubai.

Honduras shows the other end of the range. In 2013 the country changed its constitution to allow Zones for Employment and Economic Development, known as ZEDEs, areas with their own laws, courts and taxes. An earlier plan had already been struck down as a breach of sovereignty, the country's right to govern itself. Próspera, on the island of Roatán, applied in 2017. It was built with American venture capital through a Delaware company that holds a veto on its council, and it offers single-digit taxes, its own regulations and a court of retired Arizona judges who hear cases online. Neighbours in the village of Crawfish Rock feared losing their land. Then politics changed. President Xiomara Castro signed a repeal of the ZEDE law in April 2022, and on 20 September 2024 the Supreme Court declared the laws unconstitutional, with retroactive effect, according to Reuters.

Próspera's response shows what a company can do when a host reverses itself. It turned to treaty arbitration, in which a panel of arbitrators decides a dispute between an investor and a country. Its owners relied on a promise of stable rules and on CAFTA-DR, a trade treaty between the United States and Central American countries, and brought a claim at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID), a World Bank body. The claim began at about $10.775 billion. Honduras's Attorney General says it has dropped to $1.63 billion, a cut of about 85 percent. Honduras left ICSID in August 2024 and rejoined with effect from 16 August 2026. The case was still pending in October 2026, and the zone continues to operate during the dispute. An arbitration panel can award money. It cannot give a company back the power to make law on Honduran soil.

At the far end of the range sit two old cases that did produce something close to a state. Vatican City, 44 hectares inside Rome, came from the Lateran Treaty of 1929 between Italy and the Holy See, the government of the Catholic Church. The treaty recognised the Holy See's full sovereignty over the new state and settled a dispute that had lasted about 60 years, since Italian forces took Rome in 1870. The Holy See is a non-member observer state at the UN, alongside the State of Palestine. This depended on a global church and on a government that wanted to settle with it. The Sovereign Order of Malta, a Catholic order, describes itself as sovereign and reported relations with 111 countries in 2021, and it has no land except what others let it use. A new founder has neither background.

Other carve-outs are based on long custom. Mount Athos in Greece, 335 square kilometres with 20 Orthodox monasteries, governs itself under Greek law, with the monks controlling entry through a permit system. Sark, in the Channel Islands, held on to a feudal government granted in 1565 until the billionaire Barclay brothers challenged it under the European Convention on Human Rights, and a new constitution replaced it in 2008. Cherán in Mexico threw out loggers, police and politicians in 2011, and a federal Electoral Tribunal ruling that November backed its request to choose leaders by custom.

Freetown Christiania in Copenhagen shows how such room can be won from below. Squatters moved into old barracks in 1971, and the Supreme Court ruled in 1978 that the site should be cleared, an order that was never carried out. Parliament legalised the community in 1989. A 2004 Act reaffirmed the state's control, and the Supreme Court confirmed the state's full right of disposal in February 2011. So the community lost in court and then bargained. It agreed that June to set up a fund, and in July 2012 residents became legal owners of about 19 of the 84 acres. In 2013 Parliament repealed the special Christiania law, leaving the same laws as the rest of Denmark. Residents and authorities dug up the main dealing lane, Pusher Street, in 2024 after repeated shootings, which unlocked state money, and in February 2026 residents reluctantly accepted a public housing plan. About 900 people live there, half a million people visit each year, and Danish law applies.

Many announced zones have never been built, which is the common pitfall for people who invest in them. Akon City in Senegal had a promise of 2,000 acres from the president and a $6 billion price tag, and in 2025 the state agency that controlled the land said the project no longer exists. Bitcoin City in El Salvador relied on a $1 billion bond, and a later deal with the International Monetary Fund undercut the bitcoin policy behind it. It is not known to have been built. Forest City in Malaysia received a Special Financial Zone in 2024 after its Chinese developer ran into debts, with just over 1 percent of the development thought to be inhabited by one 2024 report. The Maldives Floating City was signed in 2010 and signed again in 2019, and finished homes have not been confirmed.

The same approach seems able to work at sea. Article 60(1) of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea says a coastal country may authorise artificial islands and installations in its exclusive economic zone, the belt of ocean where it controls resources. A floating city could therefore have a host's permission, on that host's terms. The Seasteading Institute and the government of French Polynesia signed a memorandum on 13 January 2017 for a floating prototype with legal semi-autonomy in the territory's waters. After a local presidential election changed the politics, the territory cut ties on 14 March 2018.

Suppose a group wants to do this today. It would need a government with a reason to agree, usually jobs or investment, and a law that its courts will uphold. It would ask for the grant to be written into the constitution, for a long promise of stable rules, and for a treaty that allows arbitration if the promise is broken, and Honduras shows that even a constitutional change can be undone. It would need to deal early with neighbours, because local land fears fed the opposition in Honduras. Its residents would keep their nationalities, and their home countries would go on taxing them where their laws do so. Banks would rely on the host's regulators, which is why a real regulator matters. This is the most workable route to separate courts and tax rules, with roughly even odds of building and funding it and somewhat under even odds of holding it through later elections. The zone stays part of the host country, so it does not produce recognition as a separate state.

inside-state.essay:
A micronation is a self-declared country, usually very small, that no government accepts as a country. The most common kind sits on land inside an existing state, such as a farm, a house, a village or a desert plot. Anyone can make such a declaration, and nothing stops it. Legally the land stays in the country whose borders surround it, and its courts go on applying its tax and criminal law to you as usual.

Founders often cite the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty. Article 1 asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other states, and Article 3 says a state's existence does not depend on recognition by others. Those tests still have to be met on land that another state does not already hold, so inside a country the territory test fails at the start. No micronation has ever become a state.

Sealand is a useful comparison. It is an old sea fort off Suffolk, declared independent in 1967. An English judge ruled in 1968 that a firearms law did not reach it, because Parliament had never extended that law beyond the three-mile limit. The fort had a real argument based on its location until Britain extended its waters to 12 miles in 1987. A farm in Australia never had that argument.

A declaration can still accomplish real things, and most of them involve attention. Protest is the first. In 1977 squatters on Freston Road in London, facing demolition, held a referendum, declared the Republic of Frestonia and applied to the United Nations. The press coverage made demolition harder, the council dropped it by 1982, and residents formed a housing co-operative that still manages homes on the site. Aramoana in New Zealand declared independence in 1980 to fight an aluminium smelter. The smelter was never built, after a partner company left. Rainbow Creek in Victoria seceded in 1979 over flooding, and the dispute was never resolved. The Principality of Wy in Sydney drew coverage in several countries in a fight over a driveway, lost its appeal in 2013, and never got the driveway.

Tourism is the second use and the most reliable. Key West's Conch Republic began in 1982 as a protest against a federal roadblock and now runs a week-long festival each April. Laàs in France, a village of 135 people, sells day trips with a customs booth and received 28 buses in 2018. Seborga in Italy has sentry boxes and an elected prince, Užupis in Vilnius stamps visitors' passports each 1 April, and Whangamomona in New Zealand holds a Republic Day festival. Art and humour are the third use, as with Lars Vilks's Ladonia in Sweden, declared in 1996 over a council's order against his sculptures, and the joke republic of Molossia in Nevada.

Now follow what happens if someone means it seriously. The first letter usually comes from the tax office. Leonard Casley declared his 75-square-kilometre wheat farm the Hutt River Province in 1970, after a quota let him sell only about 40 of his 4,000 hectares of crop. He issued passports, coins and stamps, drew a reported 40,000 tourists a year, and claimed about 14,000 citizens with 23 residents. He was prosecuted in 1977 for failing to give the Taxation Office documents. In June 2017 Justice Le Miere of the Supreme Court of Western Australia ordered him to pay more than A$2.7 million and his son more than A$242,000, saying the sovereignty argument "has no legal merit or substance". The judge added that anyone can declare themselves a sovereign in their own home "but they cannot ignore the laws of Australia or not pay tax". The principality was dissolved in August 2020, and the land was sold to settle the tax dispute. Molossia's Kevin Baugh and Zaqistan's Zaq Landsberg took another course. They pay county property tax and call it foreign aid and tributes, and their counties have no dispute with them. In the United States, claiming not to be a citizen for income tax purposes has brought criminal and civil penalties, and a return based on a position the tax agency lists as frivolous can bring a $5,000 penalty.

The courts come next, and a pattern appears. Stuart Hill, who declared the islet of Forvik in Shetland in 2008, was charged in 2011 with motoring offences on vans he called consular vehicles. He gave Lerwick Sheriff Court a 71-page argument that it had no power in Shetland. The sheriff heard it over two days, called him deluded and seriously misguided, and dismissed it. He was fined £1,400, and in December 2025 another sheriff rejected the same argument. The High Court of Australia called Casley's arguments fatuous, frivolous and vexatious, a phrase for a case with no legal merit. A court draws its power from the state that created it, so it does not treat a litigant's own declaration as a limit on that power.

Micronation founders share this ground with sovereign citizens and "freemen on the land", people who argue that the law applies to them only if they consent. In Meads v. Meads in 2012, a judge in Alberta, Canada, reviewed these arguments in detail and wrote that a decade of cases had failed to prove a single one of their concepts. No recorded case has upheld them. Trying them can make things worse. British courts have jailed such litigants for contempt or for unpaid council tax, and a Queensland court dismissed an appeal in 2020 from a man fined A$150 for driving unlicensed who said he was outside Queensland law.

Police usually arrive over cars or guns. Queensland police charged a Yidindji minister in 2015 over his own government's licence and plates. Alec Brackstone of Bumbunga claimed diplomatic immunity on a firearms charge in 1999, and the claim failed. George Muirhead declared two Queensland properties independent in 1993 to stop repossession, and police evicted him eleven days later. Force turns this into serious crime. Republic of Texas members kidnapped a couple in 1997, and their leader went to prison with a projected release date of 2041. Salvatore Meloni, who seized a private island off Sardinia in 2008, was convicted.

Money and papers cause the next problems. A declaration does not change a mortgage. The Jensen family of Snake Hill told a court in 2011 that the Bank of Queensland's foreclosure was a matter for international law, and a judge dismissed the claim. John Rudge of Avram is an unusual case. His unlicensed bank's reserves were seized, and after six cases costing about A$22 million the courts found nothing illegal and ordered them returned. Passports have done the most harm. Edwin Lipburger of Kugelmugel was sentenced to 10 weeks in Austria in 1979 for unlawful assumption of public authority. A man was arrested in Germany for trying to use a Hutt River diplomatic passport, and the Council of the European Union listed such passports as fantasy documents. Malaysia detained the daughters of the Sunda Empire's founders in 2007 for entering on its diplomatic passports. Planning law is another trap. Kugelmugel began as a house built without a permit, and a court ordered Ladonia's third sculpture removed in 1999.

Tolerance lasts as long as a project costs the government little. Their activities are usually too trivial to dispute. Hutt River's local shire listed it as having historic significance, and a state minister called its prince an enigma, while Australian diplomats exchanged 120 cables about it from 1984 to 2010. Occupying land the state wants goes differently. Alcatraz's occupiers were removed after 19 months, the Free Republic of Wendland after 33 days, and Seattle's protest zone after 23 days and two deaths. About a thousand Nigerian soldiers attacked Fela Kuti's Kalakuta compound in 1977, and it burned down.

Long survival usually needs numbers, land or a deal. Christiania in Copenhagen outlasted a 1978 Supreme Court clearance order, and residents bought part of its land in 2012. It is now under ordinary Danish law. The ZAD near Nantes stopped an airport, and many of its projects moved into ordinary French land law. Orania in South Africa bought its town and has generally been left alone. The Zapatistas have governed communities in Chiapas since a 1994 uprising. Indigenous claims such as the Murrawarri Republic and the Republic of Lakotah raise deeper arguments about land never given up. The Australian government has not acknowledged the first, and recognised tribal governments did not back the second.

The workable version is honest about what it is. Own your land, pay your taxes, follow planning rules, keep your real passport, register an association as Flandrensis and Laàs did, and label your papers as souvenirs. That can produce a good story, a festival, a campaign tool or a business. It can last for years if the state finds it harmless. It has little legal force and almost no prospect of recognition, because no state has a reason to accept part of another state on the strength of a declaration.

leases-and-extraterritorial-spots.essay:
People often imagine that an embassy, a foreign military base or an airport transit lounge is a little piece of another country, or of no country at all. The legal picture is different, and understanding it shows why these places offer so little to someone who wants a territory of their own. In almost every case the host country keeps final authority. Another country or body runs the place under a lease, a treaty or a diplomatic rule, and what that occupant can do depends on the words of the agreement.

A lease between countries works much like a lease on a flat. The owner stays the owner, the tenant gets the use of the place, and the document says how long and on what terms. Guantánamo Bay, a US naval base of 117 square kilometres in Cuba, has been held under a lease since 1903. Article III of that lease shows the idea exactly. The United States recognises "the continuance of the ultimate sovereignty of the Republic of Cuba", the final legal right to rule, while it exercises "complete jurisdiction and control" as long as it occupies the land. It began at $2,000 a year in gold and has been $4,085 a year since 1974. A 1934 treaty, in Article III, says the lease can end only if both sides agree or the United States leaves. The Cuban government that took power in 1959 says the base was imposed by force and is illegal, and it has cashed one rent cheque since then, which Fidel Castro said was deposited by mistake. The base still operates, and Cuba still objects. In Boumediene v. Bush in 2008, the US Supreme Court ruled that detainees held there have a constitutional right to challenge their detention in court, so even that base is not a place without law.

Leases can also be forced on a weaker country, and they can run out. In 1898, after China's defeat by Japan, Britain leased the New Territories of Hong Kong, including 235 islands, for 99 years with no rent. The treaty is often described as an unequal one, meaning it was forced on a weaker state. Because the lease would end on 30 June 1997, Britain and China negotiated in advance, and under their 1984 Joint Declaration all of Hong Kong passed to China. The Panama Canal Zone, 1,432 square kilometres, was granted to the United States in perpetuity, which means with no end date. It had its own governor, courts and police. Riots in 1958, 1959 and 1964 led to negotiations, and the zone was abolished in 1979. So a grant with no end date came to an end after 75 years, by a new treaty.

In all these known cases, the party receiving a lease was a country or a country-like body. The nearest thing to a private group is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order that has diplomatic relations with more than 110 countries and no land of its own. A treaty signed in 1998 gives it the upper part of Fort St Angelo in Malta for 99 years, with listed privileges and legal protections. Either side may give notice in the 50th or 75th year, with the end taking effect five years later. Malta keeps ownership, its flag flies beside the Order's, Maltese courts generally have jurisdiction, and the Order may not grant asylum there. The Order had nine centuries of history behind it and worldwide humanitarian work, and it still got a use arrangement in a fort. No new founder has come close to such a deal.

Embassies work on a different principle. Article 22 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations says embassy premises are inviolable and that the host country's officers may not enter without the consent of the head of the mission. That rule protects the work of diplomats, and it does not turn the building into foreign soil. Article 41 says people with diplomatic privileges must respect the host country's laws and that the premises must not be used in ways incompatible with the mission's functions. Julian Assange showed what the rule gives and what it leaves out. He entered Ecuador's embassy in London, a suite of rooms on the ground floor of a block of flats, on 19 June 2012, and Ecuador granted him asylum. Britain did not accept the asylum. It suggested that it could use a 1987 British law to enter, then withdrew the suggestion, and police guarded the building at a reported cost of £6.5 million in the first two years. He could not leave without being arrested, and he stayed nearly seven years. In April 2019 Ecuador's president ended the asylum and invited police in, and they arrested him. His safety depended entirely on the wishes of the government that ran the building. A private person can be there only as that government's guest, and a change of president ended it.

Airports are the place of the greatest misunderstanding. Films and news stories talk of an international zone, as if travellers past passport control had left the country. These zones are fully under the legal power of the country where they sit, and local law applies inside them. Mehran Karimi Nasseri lived in Terminal 1 of Charles de Gaulle Airport near Paris from 1988 to 2006, about 18 years, and French law applied to him throughout. Belgium and France both offered him residency, and he refused to sign because the papers did not use his chosen name. He gained no status from staying. Edward Snowden spent about a month in the transit area of Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow in 2013 after the United States revoked his passport, and he left when Russia granted him asylum. A transit area is a place people get stuck when no country will take them, and being stuck there gives them no rights over it.

Some other arrangements look similar. The UN headquarters in New York and its offices in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi are areas where the UN has been given some authority by agreement, and most local and national law still applies in them. The United States has a special visa, the C-2, so that delegates can attend meetings. The Tomb of Suleyman Shah in northern Syria was made a Turkish concession by the Treaty of Ankara in 1921, and Turkey moved it in 1973 and again in 2015, the second time on its own and over Syria's objection.

Suppose a group tried to use this route. They would first have to find a government willing to sign a lease with them on terms that give more than an ordinary tenant has. If a government offered only a normal lease, the group would be a tenant under that country's law, paying rent and tax. If it offered privileges, those would come through that country's own law or a treaty, and private groups cannot sign treaties in the sense governments use. Any term could end by notice, by a court or by the next government. Banks, insurers and suppliers would look at who holds final authority and would deal with that country's rules. Staff and residents would keep their existing citizenship and tax duties, and children born there would take their nationality from the rules of real countries.

The most workable version is a plain commercial lease of land, or a service role under a body that already has status. Either one can run for a long time. Herm, in the Channel Islands, has had tenants since 1889, and its lease was extended in 2023 to 2069. Neither gives any authority. The odds here reflect that. A lease can hold fairly well in law and in practice, and Guantánamo has lasted since 1903, but the agreement that does so is between states. Embassies and airports have sheltered people for years, and no territory passed to any of them.

add_sources.t: Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961

run-by-international-agreement.essay:
Most land on Earth belongs to one country, and that country's government makes the rules there. A small number of places have been handled differently. After a war or a long quarrel, several governments signed a treaty that took a city or a region away from any single country and placed it under an international body, a committee of foreign powers, or two countries acting together. The owner of such a place is whoever the treaty names. In the past that has been the League of Nations (the international body that came before the United Nations), the UN Security Council, a committee of foreign consuls, or a pair of neighbouring states.

The reason these places exist is usually that two or more strong countries each wanted the same spot and none could take it without a fight. Handing it to a neutral arrangement let everyone avoid losing. Danzig is the clearest example. After the First World War, Poland had been promised secure access to the sea, and the obvious port was Danzig, but about 90 percent of its people were German. So Article 100 of the Treaty of Versailles, the peace treaty with Germany, took the city from Germany, and Article 102 made it a Free City under League of Nations protection. It covered 1,952 square kilometres and held 366,730 people in 1923. It had its own parliament and its own currency, while a League High Commissioner watched over it and Poland handled its foreign relations and defence and ran its railways and post.

Tangier followed the same logic. France and Spain both wanted this Moroccan port on the Strait of Gibraltar, and Britain wanted it neutral, so the three signed a convention in Paris in December 1923. The zone covered 373 square kilometres and began operating in June 1925. An appointed assembly made laws, a committee of foreign consuls supervised it, and a Mixed Court with judges named by five European countries replaced the separate courts each foreign power had run. The zone had no tariffs, exchange controls or income taxes, and it held 85 banks by 1950. People who dream of a low-tax free territory sometimes point to it. Those low taxes were possible because several governments had agreed to allow them and kept foreign consuls in charge.

Other treaties used the same tool for a set period. The Saar Basin, a coal-mining area between Germany and France, was taken out of German government for 15 years by Article 49 of the Treaty of Versailles and held in trust by the League. A five-member commission alone made the law there, and a regional council could only advise. At the end of the 15 years, on 13 January 1935, residents voted, and 90.8 percent chose Germany. The Memel Territory on the Baltic was handed by Article 99 to the victorious Allies, who ran it through French officials until Lithuanian militias seized it in January 1923. A convention in 1924 accepted the seizure, and a German ultimatum took the territory away in March 1939.

The UN later took on similar jobs. The Free Territory of Trieste was created by the 1947 peace treaty with Italy and accepted by the Security Council in Resolution 16, as a neutral state under the Council's direct responsibility. The Council had to appoint a governor, and it never did. The Soviet Union rejected 12 nominees between October 1947 and March 1948, and the post stayed empty. The territory stayed split between Allied and Yugoslav military rule for seven years, and in 1954 a memorandum signed in London divided it between Italy and Yugoslavia. A plan for Jerusalem, called the corpus separatum (Latin for separated body), went further on paper. The General Assembly adopted it in 1947, with a UN-appointed governor and a referendum after ten years. It was never carried out, because the 1948 war left the city divided between Israel and Transjordan. Resolution 1244 placed Kosovo under UN administration from 1999, and a UN authority ran Eastern Slavonia, a region of Croatia, from January 1996 to January 1998 with about 4,800 soldiers, so that it could return to Croatia without more fighting.

A related form is the condominium, a territory governed jointly by two or more powers. New Hebrides, now Vanuatu, was shared by Britain and France from 1906 to 1980. Brčko District in Bosnia and Herzegovina, created on 8 March 2000, has 493 square kilometres and 83,516 people, and it is held jointly by the country's two internal entities because its population is mixed. Andorra, in the Pyrenees, is a sovereign state whose head of state is shared by two foreigners by virtue of their offices, the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell.

The record shows how these places end. They last as long as the powers that signed keep agreeing. Germany annexed Danzig on 1 September 1939, the day it attacked Poland. Tangier returned to Morocco by a protocol signed in October 1956, once France and Spain had ended their rule over the country. The Saar and Eastern Slavonia ended as designed, by a vote and by a handover. Trieste never began to work as intended. Only Brčko and the Andorran arrangement continue today in the forms described here.

Suppose a group of private people wanted to set up a territory this way. They would need a treaty, or a decision of the UN Security Council, and they have no standing to obtain either. A treaty in the legal sense is an agreement between countries, and an agreement signed by a private group would look to governments like a private contract. A Security Council decision needs nine of 15 votes and no veto from any of the five permanent members. Nothing in the history shows any of those bodies acting at the request of founders. They acted because governments had a dispute to settle, usually at the end of a war. A person cannot start this process, and the people living in these places did not choose the arrangement either. The residents of Danzig and Trieste were placed under it by others.

A common misunderstanding is that an international territory is free of national law and open to anyone with a good plan. These places had a great deal of law, written by foreign governments, with foreign officials enforcing it. Residents did not get a say in the basic structure. In the Saar, an elected council could offer only advice for 15 years. Another misunderstanding is that a treaty guarantees survival. It gives strong legal standing while the signatories honour it, which is why a place like this rates fairly well on law and holding on to land. Those odds stay middling, since each case ended or was altered when the powers behind it changed course.

The most workable version open to an ordinary person is to take part in such a place as a resident or to work for a government or citizens' group pressing for one as a settlement to a dispute. Local people can have influence at the moments when a treaty offers a vote, as Saar residents did in 1935. A new territory created in this way is very unlikely to be started by a private founder, and it would become recognised as a separate state only rarely. Its existence would depend on outside powers from its first day to its last.

secession-and-decolonisation.essay:
Almost every country that has joined the world map in the past hundred years got there in one of two ways. A colony or an administered territory came out from under its ruler, or part of an existing country broke away from the rest. These are the routes that have actually produced new states, so they deserve careful study. They also need something a private founder does not have, an existing people living on a territory who want to govern themselves. The land belongs to the existing country unless it agrees to let go or loses control.

The idea behind these routes is that a people can decide its own political future. International law has treated colonies and similar territories as a special case. The UN keeps a list of non-self-governing territories, places whose people have not yet governed themselves, and Western Sahara is still on it. In its Chagos opinion of 25 February 2019, the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, called General Assembly Resolution 1514 a defining moment in state practice on decolonisation. It found that Britain's separation of the Chagos Archipelago from Mauritius before independence made that decolonisation unlawful, because a people's right covers its territory as a whole. Three small Pacific countries show how a territory can leave such status on negotiated terms. The Marshall Islands, Micronesia and Palau were part of a UN trust territory run by the United States, and each chose to become a sovereign state, a self-governing country in law, while signing a compact giving the United States authority over its defence in exchange for guaranteed money. Those compacts took effect in 1986 and 1994 and have no end date, though the economic terms are renewed.

Part of an ordinary country stands in a harder position. The leading explanation is the Supreme Court of Canada's 1998 Reference re Secession of Quebec. The court held that Quebec cannot leave on its own under Canada's constitution, since secession would need a constitutional amendment. It held that international law gives no general right to break away, and it limited any such right to narrow situations such as colonial rule or foreign occupation. A state that governs all its people without discrimination keeps its territorial integrity. The court added that a clear majority on a clear question would oblige the rest of Canada to negotiate, while a majority alone has no legal effect and cannot dictate the terms. Canada's Parliament then passed the Clarity Act. An independence referendum is a public vote in which residents decide whether their territory should become a separate country. A Yes does not always bring independence. A count of Wikipedia's table as it stood in November 2026 gives about 123 votes since 1817. Of these, 59 ended in a No, 31 in a Yes followed by a recognised state, 12 in a Yes with control on the ground and no or partial recognition, and 16 in a Yes with no independence. Western Australia voted Yes in 1933 and stayed in Australia. Nevis voted Yes in 1998 and fell short of the two-thirds it needed.

What separates success from failure is mostly whether the parent country has agreed, or has lost the power to refuse. South Sudan's vote came from the 2005 peace agreement that ended a long war, which fixed the terms and date in advance. Turnout had to reach 60 percent. In January 2011, 98.83 percent chose separation, and South Sudan joined the UN that July. Montenegro used a right written into the constitution of its union with Serbia. A disputed rule required 55 percent, and Yes got 55.5 percent in 2006, by 230,711 votes to 184,954. All five permanent Security Council members accepted the result within two days. Eritrea had already defeated Ethiopian forces when it voted under UN observers in 1993, and 99.83 percent chose independence. Timor-Leste voted in 1999 under a UN mission after Indonesia's president agreed to the vote, 78.5 percent rejecting autonomy. Militias then carried out mass violence, and an Australian-led force restored order before independence in 2002.

Scotland shows the agreed route ending in a No. The Scottish and UK governments signed the Edinburgh Agreement in 2012, which temporarily gave the Scottish Parliament power to hold the vote, and 55.3 percent voted No in 2014. On 23 November 2022 the UK Supreme Court ruled that the Scottish Parliament cannot hold another one on its own, and the UK government has refused to transfer the power again. Bougainville shows that even a huge majority can be left waiting. It voted 98.31 percent for independence in 2019, under a peace agreement that made the result non-binding, and Papua New Guinea's parliament has the final decision. As of November 2026 no date for that decision had been reported, and the parties dispute the majority required. New Caledonia had three agreed votes. Independence lost by 57 percent and 53 percent, and in 2021 No took 96.5 percent under a boycott by Kanak leaders, who had asked for a delay after a COVID-19 outbreak. Riots in May 2024 killed 14 people, and its status remains under talks.

Without consent, the parent country has many tools, and they come in a rough order. The courts come first. Catalonia's parliament approved a referendum law on 6 September 2017, and Spain's Constitutional Court suspended it the next day and declared it void that October. Police come next. National officers used force at polling stations on 1 October, when Yes took 90.18 percent on a turnout of 43.03 percent. Then the government takes over. On 27 October the Catalan parliament declared independence, and the same day Spain's Senate approved direct control under Article 155 of the constitution. No state recognised the declaration. Criminal cases followed, and an amnesty for crimes linked to the referendum passed in 2024.

Beyond that lies war. Biafra declared independence from Nigeria in 1967, five states recognised it, and around two million civilians are estimated to have died before it surrendered in 1970. Katanga broke away from Congo in 1960, funded by a mining company with exclusive copper rights, and UN forces ended it by January 1963. In the United States, the Republic of New Afrika claimed five southern states in 1968, and it declined in the early 1970s after raids and mass arrests that jailed its leaders.

A common misunderstanding concerns the International Court of Justice's 2010 opinion on Kosovo. Serbia asked whether Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence broke international law, and the court found by 10 votes to 4 that it did not. That means that international law contains no ban on writing and issuing such a declaration. It does not mean that the declaration creates a state, or that other countries must accept it. Kosovo is recognised by 110 UN members, and 8 others have withdrawn recognition. It belongs to the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, and it is not a UN member, because admission needs Security Council approval with no veto. Kosovo also came out from a NATO-backed UN administration, under Security Council Resolution 1244, which few other territories have behind them. Abkhazia and South Ossetia show the limits of having a strong backer. Russia recognised both in 2008 after a war with Georgia, and only a handful of others followed. Abkhazia depends on Russia for about half its budget, and most residents use Russian passports. The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic is a full member of the African Union and is recognised by somewhere between 33 and 46 UN members, and Morocco holds most of its land, with the promised referendum never held.

Suppose a real region with a real movement wanted to try this. The stages are a long political campaign, a popular mandate shown in elections, talks with the parent country for a binding vote, then negotiation over debts, borders, currency and citizens after a Yes. Abyei in South Sudan shows how a border question can remain open for years. Puntland in Somalia shows another path, self-government since 1998 without any claim to be a separate country. A private founder cannot do this. No one can buy a population's consent, and this is why the chance of a founder creating a state this way is only about 3 percent, even though the same route gives a real population much better odds. The title that results, once it is agreed, is about as strong as title gets, and the existing odds for law and for holding the land reflect that.

unrecognised-state.essay:
Some places run themselves like countries without being accepted as countries. They have a president, a parliament, police, sometimes a currency and an army. A recognised country still holds legal title to the land, while a local government actually runs it. The ownership is therefore disputed. Somaliland, Transnistria, Northern Cyprus and Taiwan are the best known examples, and each is far from what a private founder could create, since all the current cases came out of collapse, war or foreign protection.

To follow how these places work, it helps to separate two questions. One is whether a place meets the practical tests of being a state. The usual checklist is Article 1 of the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty, which asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other states. Article 3 adds that a state's political existence does not depend on recognition by others. The other question is whether other countries accept it, which is called recognition. Recognition is a political decision made government by government, and no court or agency hands it out. A place can pass the first test and fail the second for decades.

Somaliland is the example most often given. It was a British protectorate that united with Somalia in 1960. A war against the government of Siad Barre ended in a declaration of independence in 1991, as Somalia fell into civil war. Since then it has held its own elections and issued its own currency, and it governs most of the land it claims in relative peace, with about 6.2 million people on 176,120 square kilometres. Somalia still claims it. No country recognised it for 34 years, partly because, according to The New York Times, other governments fear recognition could encourage secession elsewhere. On 26 December 2025 Israel became the first UN member to recognise it, and as of October 2026 it remained the only one. That shows how slowly the second question moves, even where the first is well answered.

The UN Security Council can actively keep a place out. When the northern third of Cyprus declared independence in 1983, nine years after Turkey invaded following a Greek-backed coup, Resolution 541 called the declaration legally invalid and asked UN members not to recognise it. Only Turkey does. Other countries treat the area as Republic of Cyprus territory under Turkish occupation. Courts abroad have applied this. In Loizidou v. Turkey in 1996, the European Court of Human Rights refused to give legal effect to a Northern Cyprus constitutional clause taking over abandoned property, because the international community does not regard the north as a state. The owner kept her title, and Turkey was held responsible because its army had effective control of the area. So a local government's laws may bind people on the ground and still mean nothing to a foreign court. So the north relies on Turkey for economic, political and military support, and its trade goes through Turkey. Trade shows what this means day to day. In the Anastasiou case in 1994, the European Court of Justice held that British authorities need not accept plant health certificates issued by Northern Cyprus, because the system relies on cooperation between recognised authorities. Exporters then shipped through a Turkish port to get Turkish papers, with delays that can spoil perishable goods. This dependence is the usual price. Other governments' refusal of recognition cuts a place off from treaties, banks and UN bodies, and it then needs one patron for what ordinary countries get from many sources.

Consider what daily life looks like. Transnistria, legally part of Moldova, has run its own government, parliament, army, police and post office since a 1992 war, in which Russian troops already stationed there took the separatists' side and about 1,000 people died. Its central bank issues a ruble that can be exchanged only inside the territory. Its citizenship papers are not accepted abroad, so many residents hold Moldovan citizenship, and many also hold Russian, Romanian or Ukrainian passports. Its population fell from 555,347 in 2004 to 475,373 in 2015. Even Russia, which keeps soldiers there, does not recognise it as a state. The money, travel and treaty problems fall on ordinary people, who work around them by keeping a second nationality from a real country.

Rights can be a further problem. A Transnistrian resident told Deutsche Welle he was arrested four times for disrespecting state order. In September 2024 its parliament made public use of the name Transnistria punishable by a fine or up to 15 days in jail.

Force remains the biggest risk, because the recognised country never gave up its claim. Artsakh, the ethnic Armenian government in Nagorno-Karabakh, won a war in 1994 and ran its own president, parliament and elections for about 30 years, relying on Armenia, which never formally recognised it. No UN member did. Azerbaijan retook most of the land in 2020, blocked the only road in December 2022 and attacked in September 2023. Almost the entire population left for Armenia within days, in what is widely described as an effective expulsion, and the president signed a decree dissolving all state institutions. Since other states had not recognised Artsakh, Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, the ban on force against a state, gave it no obvious protection, and Azerbaijan was acting on land the world accepted as its own. Rojava in north-eastern Syria, a Kurdish-led administration from 2012, lost most of its land to a Syrian offensive in January 2026 and merged into the Syrian state that August.

A different arrangement can give stability without a claim to be a separate country. Wa State in Myanmar signed a ceasefire in 1989 and has run its own army and administration since then, with the Chinese yuan as money and electricity from Chinese companies. It accepts Myanmar's sovereignty on paper, and Myanmar's 2008 constitution recognises the northern part as a self-administered area. Part of its early income came from opium and heroin, and thousands are reported to have died when 80,000 former opium farmers were forcibly moved between 1999 and 2002. Taiwan sits at the other extreme. It has about 23.3 million people, and its government was a founding member of the UN until the 1971 vote gave China's seat to Beijing. The People's Republic of China refuses relations with any country that recognises Taiwan, so states have to choose, and 11 UN members and the Holy See recognise it. A population of that size has not been enough to change this.

A person might think that any group could copy these cases by holding land long enough. The cases do not support that. Each began with an existing people in a territory, with fighters or a foreign army, at a moment when a state was collapsing. Somaliland came from a civil war, Transnistria from the end of the Soviet Union, Northern Cyprus from an invasion. A private group that buys land inside a country and declares independence would meet police and tax officers. If it took up arms, it would be charged under ordinary criminal law. None of this can be bought. For that reason the chance of building one from nothing is put at about 3 percent.

The other figures reflect those places that already exist. They hold their land fairly well, with odds near even, and their law is firm in their own courts. Recognition stays rare at about 15 percent, with Israel's move on Somaliland as the single recent gain after 34 years of self-rule, and Artsakh as the reminder that a government can run for decades and end within days. For someone already living in one of these places, the realistic approach has been to keep a recognised passport, to rely on foreign currency and patrons, and to expect that the status question may outlast a lifetime. For an outsider, these places teach mainly what full statehood costs, and show that recognition by even one UN member can take a generation.
